newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon ceasefire committee meets after clashes.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon ceasefire committee meets after clashes.

text.p: A five-nation committee monitoring a ceasefire understanding in Lebanon met on Sunday to consider Israeli and Lebanese complaints following clashes between Israeli troops and Hizbollah guerrillas.

Security sources said the representatives of the United States, France, Syria, Lebanon and Israel began the meeting in the morning in the coastal town of Naqoura, to consider a complaint by Beirut that Israel shelled civilian areas on a guerrilla-held mountain ridge on Thursday.
Israel had said it would complain that guerrillas fired on its forces from inside three villages in the area that day.

It was the fourth meeting of the committee set up to deal with violations of a U.S.-brokered ceasefire understanding that ended a 17-day Israeli blitz in April against Hizbollah after exchanges of fire that targeted civilian areas on both sides.

The agreement bars the targeting or launching of attacks from civilian areas by Israeli forces or the pro-Iranian fighters. Some 200 Lebanese, mostly civilians, were killed in the April blitz, dubbed by Israel "Operation Grapes of Wrath".

According to witnesses, some 50 shells slammed into the villages of Ain Bouswar and Jba'a on the Iqlim al-Toufah ridge, controlled by Hizbollah guerrillas, during Thursday's exchange of fire. A civilian woman in Jba'a was hurt by flying debris caused by an exploding shell.
Two Israeli soldiers were killed and eight wounded in Thursday's fighting. Two Hizbollah guerrillas were also killed.

Hizbollah (Party of God) fighters, who have killed 20 Israeli soldiers this year in south Lebanon, are battling to oust the Israeli forces from the 15-km (nine-mile)-deep zone stretching along the border from Mount Lebanon in the east to the Mediterranean westwards.

The London-based Lebanese daily al-Hayat said on Sunday that Lebanon had lodged a second complaint with the committee against Israel for allegedly kicking out two Lebanese families from the border anti-guerrilla strip it occupies in south Lebanon.

The committee met a day after Israeli jets and artillery blasted targets of the Shi'ite Moslem guerrillas in Iqlim al-Toufah in retaliation for a guerrilla raid against an Israeli patrol in which one Israeli officer was wounded.
The ceasefire understanding does not bar guerrilla assaults on Israeli forces in south Lebanon and gives both sides the right to self-defence.

Naqoura, where the committee convened in an introductory meeting for the first time on August 8, is headquarters of the U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and is five km (three miles) north of Israel.

The committee met again on August 15 to look into an Israeli complaint about what it said was the killing of a Lebanese civilian by a Hizbollah bomb, a complaint Beirut dismissed as invalid. It met on September 1 to discuss another Israeli complaint against guerrilla firing in which Israel said two Lebanese residents of the zone were wounded.

Before Sunday's meeting, Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said Saturday's Israeli strikes in south Lebanon were "necessary operations" in retaliation for attacks on Israeli forces by Hizbollah.

"We are trying in every possible way to lower the tension in the region. We have no intention of taking extraordinary measures, but we have the obligation to take every necessary operation for the good of our forces working in Lebanon," Mordechai told Israel's Channel One television.
